notes.text: That he should be the father of many nations, ver.4. 6. and in token of that his name was changed, ver. 5.
That God would be a God to him and his seed, and would give them the land of Canaan, ver. 7, 8. and the seal of this part of the covenant was circumcision, ver. 9-14.

That he should have a son by Sarai, and in token of that her name was changed, ver. 15, 16. This promise Abraham received, ver. 17. And his request for Ishmael, (ver. 18.) was answered abundantly to his satisfaction, ver. 19-22. III. The circumcision of Abraham and his family, according to God's appointment, ver. 23-27.

1. And when Abram was ninety nine years old - Full thirteen years after the birth of Ishmael. So long the promise of Isaac was deferred;

1. Perhaps to correct Abram's over-hasty marrying of Hagar.

2. That Abram and Sarai being so far striken in age, God's power in this matter might be the more magnified. The Lord appeared unto Abram - In some visible display of God's immediate glorious presence with him. And said, I am the Almighty God - By this name he chose to make himself known to Abram, rather than by his name Jehovah, Exod. vi, 3. He used it to Jacob, chap. xxxv, 11. They called him by this name, chap. xxviii, 5; xliii, 14; xlviii, 3. It is the name of God that is mostly used throughout the book of Job, at least 30 times in the discourses of that book, in which Jehovah is used but once. After Moses, Jehovah is more frequently used, and this very rarely. I am El-Shaddai. It speaks the almighty power of God, either

1. As an avenger, from |wrv| he destroyed, or laid waste; so some: and they think God took this title from the destruction of the old world: Or,

2. As a benefactor, |v| for |rva| who, and |yr| it sufficeth. Our old English translation reads it here, very significantly, I am God All- sufficient. The God with whom we have to do, is self-sufficient; he hath every thing, and he needs not any thing. And he is enough to us, if we be in covenant with him; we have all in him, and we have enough in him; enough to satisfy our most enlarged desires; enough to supply the defect of every thing else, and to secure us happiness for our immortal souls. But the covenant is mutual, walk before me, and be thou perfect - That is, upright and sincere. Observe,

1. That to walk before God, is to set God always before us, and to think, and speak, and act, in every thing as those that are always under his eye. It is to have a constant regard to his word, as our rule, and to his glory, as our end, in all our actions. It is to be inward with him in all the duties of religious worship, and to be entire for him in all holy conversation.

2. That upright walking with God is the condition of our interest in his all-sufficiency. If we neglect him, or dissemble with him, we forfeit the benefit of our relation to him.

3. A continual regard to God's all-sufficiency will have a great influence upon our upright walking with him.

3. And Abram fell on his face while God talked with him - Either,

1. As one overcome by the brightness of the Divine glory: Daniel and John did so likewise. Or.

2. As one ashamed of himself, and blushing to think of the honours done to one so unworthy. He looks upon himself with humility, and upon God with reverence, and, in token of both, falls on his face.

4. The promise is here introduced with solemnity: As for me, saith the Great God, Behold, behold and admire it, behold and be assured of it, my covenant is with thee. And thou shalt be a father of many nations - This implies,

1. That his seed after the flesh should be very numerous, both in Isaac and in Ishmael, and in the sons of Keturah. And the event answered, for there have been, and are, more of the children of men descended from Abraham, than from any one man at equal distance with him from Noah, the common root.

2. That all believers, in every age, should be looked upon as his spiritual seed, as the father of the faithful. In this sense the apostle directs us to understand this promise, Rom. iv, 16, 17. He is the father of those, in every nation, that, by faith, enter into covenant with God, and (as the Jewish writers express it) are gathered under the wings of the divine majesty.

5. In token of this, his name was changed from Abram, a high father, to Abraham, the father of a multitude. This was to confirm the faith of Abraham, while he was childless; perhaps even his own name was sometimes an occasion of grief to him; Why should he be called a high father, who was not a father at all? But now God had promised him a numerous issue, and had given him a name which signified so much; that name was his joy.

And I will establish my covenant — Not to be altered or revoked; not with thee only, then it would die with thee but with thy seed after thee; and it is not only thy seed after the flesh, but thy spiritual seed. It is everlasting in the evangelical meaning of it. The covenant of grace is everlasting; it is from everlasting in the counsels of it, and to everlasting in the consequences of it; and the external administration of it is transmitted, with the seal of it, to the seed of believers, and the internal administration of it by the Spirit to Christ's seed in every age. This is a covenant of exceeding great and precious promises. Here are two which indeed are all-sufficient, that God would be their God. All the privileges of the covenant, all its joys, and all its hopes, are summed up in this. A man needs desire no more than this to make him happy. What God is himself, that he will be to his people: wisdom to guide and counsel them, power to protect and support them, goodness to supply and comfort them; what faithful worshippers can expect from the God they serve, believers shall find in God as theirs. This is enough, yet not all.

Sarah shall her name be — The same letter is added to her name that was to Abraham's. Sarai signifies my princess, as if her honour were confined to one family only: Sarah signifies a princess, viz. of multitudes.

glossa.text: . . . . . . « And I will set my covenant, » etc. In the Hebrew *berith* ( ), which signifies not a testament, but a covenant, or a compact.

« Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram. » ((HIERON.)) The Hebrews say that God added out of his own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton, the letter *h* to Abraham and to Sara. Now he was called Abram, which is *an exalted father;* afterward he was called Abraham, which is *a father of many,* for *of nations* is not had in the name, but is understood. Nor is it to be wondered at that, whereas among the Greeks and among us the letter *a* seems to have been added, the letter *h* is said to have been added: for it is the idiom of the Hebrew tongue to write *h* and to read *a*: as, on the contrary, to pronounce *h* and to write *a*.

« Sarai thy wife, » etc. ((ISID.)) The promise concerning the calling of the Gentiles is declared in Isaac, the son of promise, that is, of grace, not of nature, since he is of an aged father and a barren mother: and because this was to be not by generation, as Ismael was, but by regeneration, circumcision was commanded, when the son of Sara is promised in the type of the Church, not when Ismael is, who is the type of the Jews.

((HIERON.-ISID.)) They err who think that Sara was at first written with one *r*, and that afterward another *r.* was added. And because *r* among the Greeks signifies *a hundred*, they surmise many follies about this name, whereas, however they may wish the word to have been changed, it ought to have not a Greek but a Hebrew reckoning. For it is Hebrew. For no one, calling anyone whatsoever in one language, takes the etymology of the word from another. Sarai therefore was at first called ( ) by *scin, res, iod.* When therefore the *iod* was taken away, the letter *he* was added, which is read for *a*, and she was called *Sara* ( ). For before she was called *my princess,* because she was as it were the mother of one family: afterward, absolutely, *a princess,* being namely about to be princess of all nations. Some most wretchedly surmise that she was first called *leprosy,* and afterward *a princess,* since leprosy is called *sarai* ( ), which in our tongue seems to have some likeness, but in the Hebrew is utterly different. For it is written by *zadich* and *ain* and *res* and *tau;* which manifestly differs from the three above, that is, *schin, res* and *he,* by which *Sara* is written.

notes.text: Abhorred — He did not turn away his face from it, as men do from things which they abhor. From him - For ever: tho' he did so for a time.
Great congregation — In the universal church, of Jews and Gentiles.

Satisfied — This is doubtless to be understood, of those spiritual blessings, that grace and peace, and comfort, which all believing souls have in the sense of God's love, the pardon of their sins, and the influences of God's spirit. Seek him - That seek his favour. Your heart - He speaks of the same persons still, though there be a change from the third to the second person, as is usual in these poetical books. For ever - Your comfort shall not be short and transitory, as worldly comforts are, but everlasting.

The world — All nations from one end of the world to the other. So this is an evident prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles, and a clear proof, that this psalm immediately speaks of Christ; to whom alone, this and divers other passages of it, belong. Remember - They shall remember their former wickedness with grief and shame, and fear; particularly in worshiping dead and impotent idols. They shall remember their great and manifold obligation to God, which they had quite forgotten, his patience in sparing them so long, in the midst of all their impieties, and in giving his son for them: they shall remember the gracious words and glorious works of Christ, what he did, and suffered for them; which possibly divers of them had been eye and ear-witnesses of. The Lord - Into the only true God, and unto Jesus Christ, to whom this name of Jehovah is often ascribed in scripture.
For — This is added as a reason, why the Gentiles should be converted, because God is not only God and the Lord of the Jews, but also of the Gentiles, and of all nations.

Fat — Kings and princes, and the great men of the world. Shall eat - Shall feed upon the bread of life, Christ and all his benefits. Worship - This is added to shew what kind of eating he spoke of. Go down - That is, all mankind, for none can escape death.

A seed — Christ shall not want a seed or posterity, for though the Jewish nation will generally reject him, the Gentiles shall come in their stead. A generation - That believing seed shall be reputed both by God and men, The generation, or people of the Lord, as the Jews formerly were.

They — The seed last mentioned. Come - From Judea and Jerusalem (from whence the gospel was first to go forth) to the Gentile world, to the several parts whereof the apostles went upon this errand. His - God's righteousness: his wonderful grace and mercy unto mankind, in giving them Christ and the gospel; for righteousness is often put for mercy or kindness. Unto - Unto succeeding generations. Whereby David gives us a key to understand this psalm, and teaches us that he speaks not here of himself, but of things which were to be done in after-ages, even of the spreading of the gospel among the Gentiles, in the time of the New Testament. That he - They shall declare that this is the work of God, and not of man. David extolls the goodness of God as his shepherd, and expresses his confidence in him, ver. 1-6. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *Ye that fear the Lord, praise him,* etc. ((CASS.)) Human fear brings forth not praise, but blame.

*Let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he hath not despised,* etc. Whom he means by the seed of Jacob he opens, adding: *Of the poor man.* ((AUG.)) Not of him who cries out with the words of sins out of a vain life, but of him who is not swollen with the pomps of the world.
*With thee is my praise in a great church,* etc. ((ID.)) He places his praise with God, who teaches that there be no presuming in man.

*They shall praise the Lord that seek him: they shall live.* ((ID.)) The poor are rich in God: therefore poor, because they praise God that they may seek him, and he himself is the riches of the poor. *Their hearts shall remember for ever and ever, and shall be converted to the Lord.* ((ID.)) Because he is the food of the heart.

*They have eaten and have adored.* ((ID.)) Let not the dispenser forbid to eat, but let him warn the exactor to fear. *In his sight shall they fall.* ((CASS.)) The Church receives both, but he himself sees and discerns.

*It shall be shewn,* etc. ((ID.)) Or to the angels, who offer the prayers of men to God, not for instruction, but for ministry.

((CASS.)) Note that the psalms of the passion end in the great hope of Christians, that it may be known that salvation is from the passion.

notes.text: The promise, that he should be the heir of the world — Is the same as that he should be "the father of all nations," namely, of those in all nations who receive the blessing. The whole world was promised to him and them conjointly. Christ is the heir of the world, and of all things; and so are all Abraham's seed, all that believe in him with the faith of Abraham
If they only who are of the law — Who have kept the whole law. Are heirs, faith is made void - No blessing being to be obtained by it; and so the promise is of no effect.

Because the law — Considered apart from that grace, which though it was in fact mingled with it, yet is no part of the legal dispensation, is so difficult, and we so weak and sinful, that, instead of bringing us a blessing, it only worketh wrath; it becomes to us an occasion of wrath, and exposes us to punishment as transgressors. Where there is no law in force, there can be no transgression of it.

Therefore it — The blessing. Is of faith, that it might be of grace - That it might appear to flow from the free love of God, and that the promise might be firm, sure, and effectual, to all the spiritual seed of Abraham; not only Jews, but gentiles also, if they follow his faith.

Before God — Though before men nothing of this appeared, those nations being then unborn. As quickening the dead - The dead are not dead to him and even the things that are not, are before God. And calling the things that are not - Summoning them to rise into being, and appear before him. The seed of Abraham did not then exist; yet God said, "So shall thy seed be." A man can say to his servant actually existing, Do this; and he doeth it: but God saith to the light, while it does not exist, Go forth; and it goeth. Gen. xvii, 5. 18-21. The Apostle shows the power and excellence of that faith to which he ascribes justification. Who against hope - Against all probability, believed and hoped in the promise. The same thing is apprehended both by faith and hope; by faith, as a thing which God has spoken; by hope, as a good thing which God has promised to us. So shall thy seed be - Both natural and spiritual, as the stars of heaven for multitude. Gen. xv, 5.
On his account only — To do personal honour to him.

But on ours also — To establish us in seeking justification by faith, and not by works; and to afford a full answer to those who say that, " to be justified by works means only, by Judaism; to be justified by faith means, by embracing Christianity, that is, the system of doctrines so called." Sure it is that Abraham could not in this sense be justified either by faith or by works; and equally sure that David (taking the words thus) was justified by works, and not by faith. Who raised up Jesus from the dead - As he did in a manner both Abraham and Sarah. If we believe on him who raised up Jesus - God the Father therefore is the proper object of justifying faith. It is observable, that St. Paul here, in speaking both of our faith and of the faith of Abraham, puts a part for the whole. And he mentions that part, with regard to Abraham, which would naturally affect the Jews most.
Who was delivered — To death. For our offenses - As an atonement for them. And raised for our justification - To empower us to receive that atonement by faith.

glossa.text: *For not through the law was the promise.* Other promises were made to Christ than to Abraham. For to Abraham they were made thus, that those who should imitate him in that manner would be blessed by Christ; but to Christ not so, but so that he should not only be the exemplar and form of the ordering of morals and of works, but that he should bless with an eternal blessing those who imitate him. *To his seed.* That is, to all believers who are the seed of Abraham, not by flesh, but by imitation. Or to Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made, because it was to be fulfilled in him.

*For if,* etc. As if he should say: Truly Abraham is not the heir of the world through the law: because his sons through the law are not those sons who are called heirs, namely as possessing what he himself has. For if this were so, these incongruities would follow from it: that faith would be made void, by which it stands that Abraham was just; that the promise would be abolished, that is, unfulfilled, so that there are no heirs: for the law makes no heirs, since rather it works wrath, and so transgression; for from it comes transgression, because without it there is none. Therefore, because if these things would follow from the law, then it is from faith that they are heirs, and so the promise is firm.

*The law works wrath.* That it might make offenders guilty, not by an efficient cause, but by grace not helping; or it would make them guilty by temporal punishments, it would work wrath, because [it works] transgression; and in what manner this is, he opens, saying:

*For where,* etc. ((ORIG.)) He shows that there cannot be transgression unless there has been a law; yet not that, if there is a law, there will in every kind be transgression: for it can come about that there is a law and there is no transgression, but not conversely.

*Nor transgression.* He does not say: There is no iniquity. For everyone who passes the law by is unjust, but not the contrary. For those who have not received the law can be called unjust, but they cannot be called transgressors.

*Not to him who is of the law.* Because such a man as this has fallen away from grace, and therefore for the sake of faith one must withdraw from the law, that the promise may be firm: for the law, without the grace of the promise, not only does not take away sin, but even increases it.

*Who against hope.* He begins to commend the faith of Abraham, that we may imitate him who through faith received justice and such a promise.

*So shall thy seed be,* etc. It must be known that Abraham first knew God as three and one, and through this merit of faith he obtained the remission of all sins. But after justice, he received a promise from God that he should become the father of many nations. Then again a promise was made to him that his seed should become as the stars, etc.
*He was not weakened.* Some, puffed up by the reasoning of the world, neglected God: therefore the things that are impossible to the world God did, that believing through these they might be saved.

*In the promise.* Isaac, promised against the nature of human generation, was for a sign that the Son of God was to be born of man against human nature; and that the sons of men, through the spirit of regeneration, were to be begotten out of sinners into sons of God, out of mortals into immortals.

*In him who raised up Jesus,* etc. He has fitly entered upon the discourse concerning the Lord, and says: he died not for his own sins, for in that manner he ought not to have risen again, just as neither did any man before him, but for our sins, that he might free us from them. In the same way as he also restored Abraham and the womb of Sarah, already dead through old age and barrenness, to life and to the procreation of children.

*Who was delivered up.* The death of Christ alone signifies the destruction of the old life, and in the resurrection alone is the new life signified, which begins from justification and will be perfected in immortality.

notes.text: He spake that saying openly — Or in express terms. Till now he had only intimated it to them. And Peter taking hold of him - Perhaps by the arms or clothes.
Looking on his disciples — That they might the more observe what he said to Peter.

And when he called the people — To hear a truth of the last importance, and one that equally concerned them all. Let him deny himself - His own will, in all things small and great, however pleasing, and that continually: And take up his cross - Embrace the will of God, however painful, daily, hourly, continually. Thus only can he follow me in holiness to glory.
Matt. xvi, 25; Luke ix, 24; Luke xvii, 33; John xii, 25.

Whosoever shall be ashamed of me and of my words — That is, avowing whatever I have said (particularly of self denial and the daily cross) both by word and action. Matt. x, 32; Luke ix, 26; Luke xii, 8.

glossa.text: *That it behoveth,* etc. ((HIER.)) As a skilled pilot, guarding against a storm while it is calm, wills his own sailors to be ready. As elsewhere: *If any man will come after me, let him deny himself ((Matth. XVI))*, etc.

*And taking him. ((BEDA.))* With the affection of one that loves, saying: *Far be it from thee, Lord.* Or, as it is better had in the Greek: *Be thou merciful,* etc., *as far as* and he takes hold of him into his own affection, or leads him aside, lest he seem to rebuke his master while the rest are present.

*Go behind. ((ID.))* Many think that it was not Peter, but the adversary spirit, that was corrected, at whose suggestion the Apostle said this: But to me the Apostle's error, coming from the affection of piety, will never seem the devil's prompting. To the devil it is said: *Go behind, Satan.* To Peter: *Go behind me,* etc., that is, follow my judgment.

*The things that are of God,* etc. It is my will and the Father's that I should die for the salvation of men: thou wilt not have the grain of wheat fall into the ground, that it may bring forth much fruit.

*If any man will,* etc. ((BEDA.)) After he had shown the mystery of his passion and of his resurrection, he exhorts all to imitate the example of the passion, and to all he promises the salvation of souls. But to the more perfect he disclosed how great things he was to suffer, and that he was to rise again from the dead, giving thereby a form of preaching: namely, that each be instructed according to his own measure, and that higher things be not committed to the weak.

*Let him deny himself.* He is not able to lay hold of what is beyond himself, if he has not known how to slay what he is. Unless a man fail to his own self, he does not draw near to God, who is above him. *Let him take up his cross.* Either by wearing down the body through abstinence, or the mind through compassion. Of the body Paul says: *I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection ((II Cor. IX))*, etc. The same, of compassion of mind: *Who is weak, and I am not weak? ((II Cor. XI.))*

*For he that shall be ashamed. ((BEDA.))* The Church signifies two times: one of persecution, when the soul must be laid down; the other of peace, when earthly desires must be broken.

*For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc. Because many overcome avarice and despise things that pass away, but, hindered by bashfulness, do not utter with the voice the rightness of faith which they hold. He adds: *For he that shall be ashamed of me,* etc.

echoes.text: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: 'The promise to Abraham and to his seed that he should be heir of the world' (4:13) universalizes the land-inheritance promises of Genesis (17:8 'I will give to you and your offspring... all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession'; cf. 13:15; 15:7). Paul expands the territorial 'land' to 'the world' (kosmos), a move grounded in the cosmic scope of the promise.

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”
echoes.note: The promise to Abraham 'and to his seed' (4:13) echoes the oath of Genesis 22:17-18, 'I will multiply your seed... and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed,' which links seed, multiplication, and universal blessing — the basis for 'heir of the world.' The word 'seed' (sperma) is the Genesis catchword Paul foregrounds.

echoes.text: Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit from sea to sea, And from the River to the utmost part of the earth.
echoes.note: The 'heir of the world' expansion has a Second Temple precedent in Sirach 44:21, where God promises Abraham 'to give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth' — already enlarging the land to global scope. A contested background echo for Paul's kosmos language.

echoes.text: He said to him, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
echoes.note: Genesis 15:7 ('I am the Lord who brought you out... to give you this land to inherit it'), within the same chapter as 15:6, supplies the inheritance vocabulary Paul universalizes in 'heir of the world.' Faint; reinforces that Paul reads the whole Genesis 15 unit.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim with the introductory formula 'As it is written' in 4:17: 'I have made you a father of many nations' (Genesis 17:5 LXX, 'patera pollon ethnon tetheika se'). Paul reads the perfect tense ('I HAVE made') as already-accomplished divine speech that calls the not-yet into being.

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim in 4:18: 'So will your seed be' (Genesis 15:5 LXX, 'houtos estai to sperma sou'), the star-promise spoken immediately before Genesis 15:6. Paul binds the two halves of Genesis 15 together: the promise (v.5) and Abraham's believing response reckoned as righteousness (v.6).

echoes.text: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
echoes.note: 'He being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb' (4:19) draws directly on Genesis 17:17, where Abraham, told he will have a son, says 'Shall a child be born to him who is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety, bear?' Paul reuses the numeric detail and the implied biological impossibility.

echoes.text: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
echoes.note: 'The deadness of Sarah's womb' and Abraham's 'body already worn out' (4:19) echo Genesis 18:11-12: 'it had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women,' and Sarah's words 'After I am worn out (LXX katetribe), shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' Paul's 'worn out' (nenekromenon/already dead) language tracks the Genesis 18 description of both spouses' exhaustion.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: The pericope closes in 4:22 by re-quoting the governing text: 'Therefore it also was reckoned to him for righteousness.' Recurrence of Genesis 15:6 as the inclusio binding the demonstration of Abraham's faith back to its scriptural anchor.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: Abraham 'being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform' (4:21) answers the rhetorical question of Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the Lord? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son.' Paul converts the LORD's question into Abraham's confident assent — God's power over the impossible.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) draws on the scriptural confession of God as life-giver, e.g. 1 Samuel 2:6 (Hannah), 'The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.' This is the standard OT idiom Paul applies to both Isaac's miraculous conception and the resurrection.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) also resonates with Deuteronomy 32:39, 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal,' a foundational text for God's sole power over death and life. Reinforces the same divine attribute Paul predicates.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) may figurally echo Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where the Spirit raises a dead Israel to life — a paradigm of resurrection-as-restoration. Thematically coherent with Paul's resurrection horizon; verbally faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) figurally echoes the creation account, where God's word summons being out of nonbeing ('Let there be... and there was'). Paul pairs creation (calling the nonexistent) with resurrection (giving life to the dead) as twin marks of the God Abraham believed.

echoes.text: I beseech you, my child, to lift your eyes to the heaven and the earth, and to see all things that are therein, and thus to recognize that God made them not of things that were, and that the race of men in this wise comes into being.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) has its closest Second Temple parallel in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where the mother urges her son to recognize 'that God did not make them out of things that existed' — an early articulation of creation from nothing, paired (as in Romans 4) with resurrection hope. Contested background echo.

echoes.text: Yes, my hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spread out the heavens: when I call to them, they stand up together.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) may echo the Isaianic creator who 'calls' the heavens and earth into existence (Isaiah 48:13; 41:4; 44:24), where divine calling is creative summons. Faint verbal link via the verb 'call'; marked contested.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted' (4:23-24) explicitly thematizes the act of reading Genesis 15:6 as Scripture written for the church. The verb 'accounted/reckoned' is carried forward one last time, applied now to believers in the God who raised Jesus.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'Who was delivered up for our trespasses' (4:25) echoes Isaiah 53 LXX, especially 53:6 ('the Lord delivered him up for our sins,' paredoken auton tais hamartiais hemon) and 53:12 ('he was delivered up because of their sins'). Paul's verb 'delivered up' (paredothe) plus 'for our trespasses' is verbatim Servant-song language, identifying the crucified Jesus as the suffering Servant.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'And was raised for our justification' (4:25) draws on Isaiah 53:11 LXX, 'the righteous one will justify the many (dikaiosai dikaion... tois pollois), and he shall bear their sins.' The pairing of the Servant's vindication with the justification 'of many' undergirds Paul's resurrection-justification clause, linking the Abraham-righteousness midrash to the Servant's righteousness.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him. Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted. But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we […]
echoes.note: That 'the Son of Man must suffer many things... and be killed' draws on the Servant who was 'despised and rejected,' 'a man of sorrows,' who bore suffering and was 'cut off.' The necessity (dei) of redemptive suffering coheres with Isaiah 53's vicarious death; this is the foundational suffering-text behind Mark's passion predictions.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: 'Be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the scribes' anticipates the rejected-stone of Psalm 118, which Mark quotes explicitly at 12:10 ('the stone the builders rejected'). The specific language of rejection by the leadership maps onto the builders' rejection, making this a deliberate, recurrent intertext.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: The self-designation 'Son of Man' derives from Daniel's vision of 'one like a son of man' who comes with the clouds and receives dominion. Mark's title is recurrent and load-bearing; though here paired paradoxically with suffering, the Danielic figure of vindicated dominion underlies the whole Son-of-Man complex.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people. All those who see me mock me. They insult me with their lips. They shake their heads, saying, “He trusts in Yahweh; let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
echoes.note: The motif of the righteous one despised and rejected ('a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind') feeds the suffering-Son-of-Man pattern; Mark draws heavily on Psalm 22 for the passion (15:34, 15:24), so its presence behind the first prediction is coherent and recurrent.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After three days rise again' may echo Hosea's 'after two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up.' The third-day-resurrection language is plausibly drawn from this oracle of restoration, a connection later interpreters made explicit.

echoes.text: He showed me Joshua the high priest standing before Yahweh’s angel, and Satan standing at his right hand to be his adversary. Yahweh said to Satan, “Yahweh rebuke you, Satan! Yes, Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Isn’t this a burning stick plucked out of the fire?”
echoes.note: 'Get behind me, Satan!' resonates with Zechariah's vision where 'the LORD rebuke you, O Satan' is spoken against the accuser. The act of rebuking the satan/adversary who opposes God's purpose coheres verbally and conceptually with Jesus' rebuke of Peter as voicing 'the things of men.'

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'When he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels' renders the Son of Man's coming in Daniel's vision, where the one like a son of man comes with the clouds before the Ancient of Days to receive glory and an everlasting kingdom. The conjunction of Son of Man, coming, and glory is a direct appropriation.

echoes.text: You shall flee by the valley of my mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach to Azel; yes, you shall flee, just like you fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with you./f + Septuagint reads “him” instead of “you”./f*
echoes.note: 'The LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with him' supplies the entourage of 'holy angels/holy ones' accompanying the divine advent. Mark's coming Son of Man 'with the holy angels' draws on this theophany of God arriving with his holy retinue for judgment.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire. A fiery stream issued and came out from before him: thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
echoes.note: The throne-and-myriads scene—'thousand thousands served him'—reinforces the angelic-attendant imagery of the Son of Man's glorious advent in v.38. Coherent with the Danielic court of judgment that frames being 'ashamed' before the coming one.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough, That he should live on forever, that he should not see corruption.
echoes.note: 'For what will a man give in exchange for his life?' closely parallels the psalm's reflection that no one can 'give to God a ransom for his life... for the redemption of their soul is costly.' The wisdom logic that life cannot be bought back with wealth underlies vv.36-37.

echoes.text: What does man gain from all his labor in which he labors under the sun?
echoes.note: 'What does it profit a man, to gain the whole world?' echoes Qoheleth's recurring 'What profit (yitron) has a man of all his toil?'—the wisdom idiom of weighing profit against the vanity of worldly gain. Faint but coherent with the saying's sapiential cast.

echoes.text: They have dealt corruptly with him. They are not his children, because of their defect. They are a perverse and crooked generation.
echoes.note: 'This adulterous and sinful generation' reprises the Song of Moses' 'perverse and crooked generation,' tying the audience of Jesus' words to the faithless wilderness cohort already invoked in the sign-seeking pericope. The recurrence of the 'generation' label within Mark 8 strengthens the link.

echoes.text: Contend with your mother! Contend, for she is not my wife, neither am I her husband; and let her put away her prostitution from her face, and her adulteries from between her breasts;
echoes.note: The charge 'adulterous... generation' draws on the prophetic figure of Israel as an unfaithful, adulterous spouse (Hosea's central metaphor), framing the present generation's unbelief as covenant infidelity. Faint, but within the prophetic adultery-as-apostasy tradition.

registers.label: Spare
lines: God called Abram out and gave him a new name.
By faith we are children of the promise.
If any want to follow, let them take up the cross.
We are learning to follow Jesus.
Those who lose their life for the gospel will save it.
Teach us to let go and follow.
From the ends of the earth, come, let us worship.
All the families of the earth shall bow down. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: To an old man and a barren woman, God speaks a promise and hands them new names.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
And to all who would follow, Jesus says plainly: take up your cross and come.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
It is a hard word, that to save your life you must first lose it, that the road runs through Jerusalem.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Yet the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord; every family will bow.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So shoulder what he gives you, and walk; we do not go alone.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: God gives a barren house a name and a promise.
Lead us in your way.
Take up the cross, Jesus says; come and follow.
Lead us in your way.
To save our life we must first lose it.
Lead us in your way.
From the ends of the earth, come, let us worship.
Lead us in your way. Amen.
